messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 37
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Database Administrator
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening illness
- Pcl5: 48

# Marcus

Marcus is a 37-year-old database administrator who sits with his arms crossed during most sessions, not out of hostility, but out of habit — a kind of self-containment he has practiced for the better part of two years. He is precise in the way he speaks, choosing words carefully, the way he chooses variable names at work. He does not like loose ends or ambiguity. What happened to his body two years ago was nothing but ambiguity, and he has not forgiven it.

In the spring of his thirty-fifth year, Marcus began losing weight without trying. He attributed it to stress — his marriage was fraying, his workload had doubled after a round of layoffs. Then came the fatigue that sleep could not touch, and a lymph node in his neck that his wife noticed one evening while they were watching television. He remembers her fingertips on his throat and the way her face changed. Within three weeks, he had a diagnosis: Hodgkin's lymphoma, Stage III. The oncologist used the word *treatable*, and Marcus held onto that word like a handgrip over a drop.

What followed was eight months of chemotherapy. He describes the treatment period in fragmented, almost reluctant detail — the smell of the infusion suite, a particular shade of fluorescent light, the sound of the IV pump cycling. There was one hospitalization for a severe infection when his immune system collapsed entirely. He ran a fever of 104 for three days. He remembers lying in the hospital bed at three in the morning, genuinely uncertain whether he would be alive by morning, doing arithmetic in his head — the kind of purposeless mental activity that, he now understands, was his mind trying to stay tethered to something concrete. He was thirty-five years old, and he thought he was dying alone in a beige room.

He survived. His scans came back clear. His oncologist called it an excellent response. His marriage did not survive. His wife, who had stayed through the illness with what Marcus describes as "a kind of exhausted duty," filed for divorce eight months after his final treatment. He does not blame her. He is not sure he was easy to be with even before he got sick.

Now Marcus lives alone in a one-bedroom apartment and goes to work every day and manages databases with a competence that no one would question. He is good at his job. The logic of relational databases comforts him — there are rules, there are constraints, there are defined relationships between tables. His body had none of those things. It turned on him without warning and without reason.

He does not sleep well. He wakes most nights between two and four, heart pounding, with the specific and irrational certainty that something is wrong inside him. He checks his lymph nodes. He has a protocol for this, a sequence — neck, armpits, groin — that he runs through before he can settle again. Some nights he cannot settle. He lies there cataloguing physical sensations, translating each one into either *probably nothing* or *call the doctor Monday*. He is aware this is not a sustainable system.

He avoids his annual follow-up appointments for weeks past their scheduled dates, then reschedules them, then avoids them again. He cannot fully explain this. He knows intellectually that early detection is the point of surveillance. But walking into that oncology building — the particular smell of it, the carpet pattern in the waiting room — drops him somewhere he does not want to go. He has left the parking lot twice without going inside.

He does not talk about any of this at work. His colleagues know he was sick; they sent a card. He thanked them and moved on. He keeps his screens arranged in a specific order, maintains meticulous backup schedules, documents everything. Control over systems is the one currency he still trusts. He is not sure what he is waiting for, exactly. He says he just wants to feel like the illness is behind him. He does not yet believe that it is.
